content: Erythema toxicum is a common and benign skin condition that occurs in newborns. It is not associated with cancer or any serious health issues. The primary symptom of erythema toxicum is a rash characterized by small papules that are yellow to white in color, surrounded by areas of reddened skin. The number of papules can vary, ranging from just a few to several. These lesions are most commonly found on the face and the central part of the body, but they can also appear on the upper arms and thighs. The rash is dynamic, often changing rapidly, with lesions appearing and disappearing in different areas over the course of hours to days. The exact cause of erythema toxicum remains unknown. The condition may be present within the first few hours of life, but it typically appears after the first day and can persist for several days. Although it is harmless, it can understandably cause concern for new parents. Erythema toxicum is observed in more than 50% of healthy newborns. It is most commonly seen in full-term infants, typically between the ages of 3 days and 2 weeks. Diagnosis is usually straightforward and can be made by a healthcare provider during a routine well-baby examination. No additional testing is typically required to confirm the diagnosis. If you are concerned about the condition, it is recommended to discuss it with your healthcare provider during a routine examination. However, urgent medical care is generally not necessary. Treatment is not required for erythema toxicum. The large red blotches and associated papules typically resolve on their own without any specific intervention or changes in skin care. The rash associated with erythema toxicum usually clears within two weeks. In most cases, it is completely resolved by the time the infant reaches four months of age. There are no complications associated with erythema toxicum. It is a self-limiting condition with an excellent prognosis.
